title: Matching systems and phasing lines
blurb: Tell gamma, hairpin and stub matches apart, size a quarter-wave section, and see what Wilkinson dividers and phasing lines do.

E9E01.why: A beta or hairpin match feeds a **split element insulated from the boom**. A gamma match works with the element bolted to the boom.

E9E02.why: Gamma: shield to the **center of the element**, center conductor tapped a fraction of a wavelength to one side.

E9E03.why: A **stub match** is a short length of line in parallel with the feed line at or near the feed point.

E9E04.why: The gamma rod adds inductance, so the series capacitor **cancels the unwanted inductive reactance**.

E9E05.why: A hairpin is an inductor. It cancels a **capacitive** feed point: an element shorter than ½ wavelength.

E9E06.why: Zq = √(100 × 50) = 70.7 Ω. **75 Ω** is closest: Zin = 75² ÷ 100 = 56 Ω, SWR about 1.1.
E9E06.trap: 50 Ω gives 25 Ω at the line (SWR 2).

E9E07.why: The **reflection coefficient** Γ = (Z load − Z₀) ÷ (Z load + Z₀) describes how a load meets the line.
E9E07.trap: Characteristic impedance, VF and dielectric describe the line alone.

E9E08.why: A Wilkinson divider splits power **equally between two 50 Ω loads** while the input stays 50 Ω.

E9E09.why: A **gamma match** shunt-feeds a grounded tower at its base: the tower stays grounded.

E9E10.why: A beta or hairpin match is an **inductance across the feed point**. Gamma uses a series capacitor instead.

E9E11.why: Phasing lines set each element's phase, so the signals add or cancel by direction: they **control the pattern**.
